slides.title: Old Friends, New Name
slides.kicker: Algebraic expressions you know, now with a mission.
bullets: In earlier grades you met algebraic expressions built from terms joined by plus and minus signs.
This chapter studies a special family of such expressions called linear polynomials, starting from everyday situations.
Every expression is a team of terms, and each term carries a story: boxes of pens, fences, seeds.
slides.note: Same expressions, now with a superpower.

slides.title: Raju Counts Pens, Pencils
slides.kicker: A shop, some boxes, and one neat expression.
bullets: Red boxes hold 4 pens each and blue boxes hold 5 pencils each, so x red boxes give 4x pens and y blue boxes give 5y pencils.
With 3 extra pens free, Raju's total is 4x + 5y + 3, an algebraic expression with three terms: 4x, 5y and 3.
The letters x and y are variables (the book's letter-numbers), 4 and 5 are their coefficients, and 3 is a constant.
slides.note: 4 pens per box is why the 4 sits beside x.

slides.title: Naming Every Part
slides.kicker: Four jobs inside one small expression.
bullets: In 4x + 5y + 3 the terms are 4x, 5y and 3; the variables are x and y, also called letter-numbers.
The coefficient is the number multiplying a variable: 4 for x and 5 for y.
A constant term like 3 never changes, because no variable is attached to it.
slides.note: Book's new word: variables, for our old letter-numbers.

slides.title: Fencing the Garden
slides.kicker: Wire, wood and seeds each add a term.
bullets: A garden of length l and width w needs wire fence along the length at Rs 100 per metre, costing 2l × 100 = 200l.
Wooden fence along the width costs 2w × 80 = 160w, and sowing seeds at Rs 50 per square metre costs 50 × l × w = 50lw.
Total cost is 200l + 160w + 50lw: terms 200l, 160w, 50lw with variables l and w and coefficients 200, 160 and 50.
slides.note: Fence hugs both lengths, so 2l metres of wire.

slides.title: One Wire, Many Rectangles
slides.kicker: A 20 cm wire bends into different rectangles.
bullets: Bend a 20 cm wire into a rectangle of length 7 cm and width 3 cm: the perimeter is 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 cm.
The same wire also makes a rectangle of length 5.5 cm and width 4.5 cm, so the perimeter stays 20 cm.
Changing length and width changes the shape, but the sum of all four sides is fixed by the wire.
slides.note: Try your own: length 6 cm needs width 4 cm.

slides.title: Perimeter Powers a Pattern
slides.kicker: A square's perimeter is a linear polynomial.
bullets: A square of side x has perimeter 4x, and the book calls 4x a linear polynomial in the variable x.
When the side grows from 1 to 1.5 to 2 to 2.5 to 3 cm, the perimeters run 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 cm.
Every extra 0.5 cm of side adds exactly 2 cm of perimeter: the jump never changes.
slides.note: Side badhe toh perimeter badhe, by the same step!

slides.title: The Chess Club Bill
slides.kicker: Joining fee plus Rs 50 per match.
bullets: A chess club charges Rs 200 to join plus Rs 50 per match, so m matches cost 200 + 50m rupees.
The bill runs 250, 300, 350, 400, 450 for 1 to 5 matches, rising by a constant Rs 50 each time.
200 + 50m is a linear polynomial in m, and its steady rise is what the book calls a linear pattern.
slides.note: The Rs 200 joins before even one match.

slides.title: What Makes It Linear
slides.kicker: One test: constant difference between steps.
bullets: A linear polynomial has one signature: the difference between successive values at integers is constant.
Perimeters of squares rose by 2 cm for each 0.5 cm of side; chess bills rose by Rs 50 for each extra match.
Patterns with this constant jump are called linear patterns, and straight-line graphs will show why later.
slides.note: Same-size jumps, every single time.

slides.title: Polynomial Meets Equation
slides.kicker: Equate it to a constant and solve.
bullets: Two numbers add to 64 and one is 10 more than the other: if the smaller is x, the larger is x + 10.
The condition x + (x + 10) = 64 becomes 2x + 10 = 64, and 2x + 10 is a linear polynomial.
Equating a linear polynomial in one variable to a constant gives a linear equation, here 2x = 54, so x = 27.
slides.note: The numbers are 27 and 37. Check: they add to 64.

slides.title: The Input-Output Machine
slides.kicker: Feed in x, the polynomial answers.
bullets: Think of a polynomial as a machine: for the polynomial 2x + 3, every input x produces exactly one output value.
Input x = 4 gives 2 × 4 + 3 = 11; input x = -6 gives 2 × (-6) + 3 = -9.
Substituting the value of x into the expression is all the machine does, for any x you choose.
slides.note: Negative inputs welcome; the machine never complains.

slides.title: Cost of a Journey
slides.kicker: Rs 100 to start, Rs 60 for each km.
bullets: The journey cost is modelled by the linear function C(d) = 100 + 60d, with C in rupees and d in km.
The table of values runs 100, 160, 220, 280, 340, 400 as d goes from 0 to 5 km.
Each extra km adds a fixed Rs 60, so the cost grows in equal steps.
slides.note: Even at 0 km you pay Rs 100.

slides.title: Linear Growth Defined
slides.kicker: Up by a constant over equal intervals.
bullets: Linear growth describes a linear pattern where a quantity increases by a constant amount over equal intervals.
In the journey example, d increasing by one km (an equal interval) makes C increase by Rs 60 (a constant amount).
The same story fits a plant of height 1.75 feet growing 0.5 feet each month, from Exercise Set 2.4.
slides.note: One km, Rs 60. One month, 0.5 feet. See the rhythm?

slides.title: The Shrinking Tank
slides.kicker: Water falls 0.5 m every month.
bullets: A cylindrical tank holds water 3 m deep at the start of summer, and h(t) = 3 - 0.5t gives the height after t months.
Heights run 3, 2.5, 2, 1.5, 1 m for t = 0 to 4 months, dropping by a fixed 0.5 each month.
A quantity that decreases by a constant amount over equal intervals shows linear decay.
slides.note: After 5 months only 0.5 m remains.

slides.title: Growth or Decay?
slides.kicker: The sign of the constant decides.
bullets: Linear growth and linear decay use the same idea with opposite signs: constant change over equal intervals.
Journey cost C(d) = 100 + 60d rises by 60 each km, while tank height h(t) = 3 - 0.5t falls by 0.5 each month.
A phone bought for Rs 10,000 that loses Rs 800 every year is decay in action, straight from the exercises.
slides.note: Same idea, opposite direction.

slides.title: One Rule, Two Variables
slides.kicker: Two variables, linked by one rule.
bullets: A linear relationship expresses how two variables x and y connect, written as y = ax + b.
Here a and b are fixed numbers: a scales the input x and b is the starting value added on.
Every pair (x, y) that follows the rule satisfies this one equation.
slides.note: a is the doer, b is the head start.

slides.title: Tiles Get an Equation
slides.kicker: The tile pattern returns as an equation.
bullets: In the growing pattern of square tiles, x is the number of the term and y is the number of square tiles.
The linear relationship between them is y = 2x - 1, exactly the pattern met earlier in the chapter.
Using the equation: term 1 has 1 tile, term 2 has 3 tiles, term 3 has 5 tiles, and so on.
slides.note: One rule, endless terms.

slides.title: The Telecom Bill Puzzle
slides.kicker: Two bills are enough to crack it.
bullets: A telecom company charges a fixed monthly fee plus a cost per GB, and y = ax + b should model the bill.
The student observes 10 GB cost Rs 350 and 20 GB cost Rs 550, giving 350 = 10a + b and 550 = 20a + b.
Two observations, two equations: exactly what we need to find the two unknowns a and b.
slides.note: Two clues, two unknowns.

slides.title: Solving for a and b
slides.kicker: Substitute, simplify, done.
bullets: From 350 = 10a + b write b = 350 - 10a, then substitute into 550 = 20a + b.
That gives 550 = 20a + 350 - 10a, so 550 = 10a + 350 and 10a = 200, hence a = 20.
Then b = 350 - 10a = 350 - 200 = 150, and the relationship is y = 20x + 150.
slides.note: y = 20x + 150: Rs 20 per GB, fee Rs 150.

slides.title: Reading a and b
slides.kicker: The numbers have real meaning.
bullets: In y = 20x + 150, the number 20 is the cost of each GB of data used.
The number 150 is the fixed monthly fee, paid even before any data is used.
Matching a and b to the situation is how you check that your equation tells the true story.
slides.note: Sense-check a and b against the story.

slides.title: Two Points Draw a Line
slides.kicker: Any two points will do the job.
bullets: A linear equation like y = ax + b can be plotted as a straight line on the coordinate plane.
To plot y = 2x + 1, find two points: when x = 0, y = 1 giving A (0, 1), and when x = 3, y = 7 giving B (3, 7).
Plot A and B, join them with a ruler, and extend the line in both directions.
slides.note: Graph paper makes this genuinely fun.

slides.title: Points That Obey the Rule
slides.kicker: On the line means in the equation.
bullets: Other points on y = 2x + 1 include (1, 3) and (7, 15), found by substituting each x.
A point lies on a line only if its coordinates satisfy the equation of the line.
Check (7, 15): putting x = 7 and y = 15 gives 2 × 7 + 1 = 15, so it truly sits on the line.
slides.note: If it satisfies, it sits on the line.

slides.title: Five Points, One Line
slides.kicker: y is three times x here.
bullets: Plot (-1, -3), (0, 0), (1, 3), (3, 9), (4, 12) and join (-1, -3) to (4, 12): all five points fall on one straight line.
For every point, the y-coordinate is three times the x-coordinate, so the equation of the line is y = 3x.
Spotting how y depends on x lets you write the equation without any extra formula.
slides.note: Equation guessing, detective style.

slides.title: A Line That Falls
slides.kicker: Negative a tilts the line down.
bullets: The points (-3, 6), (-2, 4), (0, 0), (1, -2), (2, -4), (3, -6) all lie on one straight line.
Here each y-coordinate is -2 times the x-coordinate, so the line is y = -2x.
Because a is negative, the line slopes downward as x grows, the picture of linear decay.
slides.note: Negative a: the line walks downhill.

flashcards.front: Raju buys x red pen boxes and y blue pencil boxes, plus 3 free pens. Total expression?
flashcards.back: 4x + 5y + 3. The 4x pens, 5y pencils and 3 free pens are the three terms.

flashcards.front: In 4x + 5y + 3, what are the coefficients of x and y?
flashcards.back: 4 and 5. Each coefficient is the number multiplying its variable.

flashcards.front: What is a variable?
flashcards.back: A letter-number, like x or y, whose value can change. The book now calls letter-numbers variables.

flashcards.front: Why does the garden seed cost come out as 50lw?
flashcards.back: Seeds cost Rs 50 per square metre and the garden area is l times w, so the cost is 50lw.

flashcards.front: A 20 cm wire is bent into different rectangles. What stays the same?
flashcards.back: The perimeter: 7 by 3 and 5.5 by 4.5 both use up exactly 20 cm of wire.

flashcards.front: What is the perimeter of a square of side x?
flashcards.back: 4x, a linear polynomial in the variable x, straight from Example 4.

flashcards.front: Chess club: Rs 200 joining fee plus Rs 50 per match. Cost after m matches?
flashcards.back: 200 + 50m rupees, a linear polynomial in m. Each match adds a constant Rs 50.

flashcards.front: What is a linear equation?
flashcards.back: A linear polynomial in one variable equated to a constant, like 2x = 54.

flashcards.front: What single feature marks a linear pattern?
flashcards.back: The difference between successive values at integers is constant, like Rs 50 per extra match.

flashcards.front: For the polynomial 2x + 3, what is the output when x = -6?
flashcards.back: -9, because 2 times -6 plus 3 equals -9.

flashcards.front: Journey cost is C(d) = 100 + 60d. What is the cost at d = 0 km?
flashcards.back: Rs 100, the fixed part of the cost before any distance is travelled.

flashcards.front: Define linear growth.
flashcards.back: A linear pattern where a quantity increases by a constant amount over equal intervals.

flashcards.front: Tank height is h(t) = 3 - 0.5t. What is h after 4 months?
flashcards.back: 3 - 0.5 × 4 = 1 m. The height drops a fixed 0.5 m each month.

flashcards.front: Define linear decay.
flashcards.back: A linear pattern where a quantity decreases by a constant amount over equal intervals.

flashcards.front: A phone bought for Rs 10,000 loses Rs 800 every year. Growth or decay?
flashcards.back: Linear decay: the value falls by a constant Rs 800 every year.

flashcards.front: What is the general form of a linear relationship between x and y?
flashcards.back: y = ax + b, where a and b are fixed numbers.

flashcards.front: The square-tile pattern has relationship y = 2x - 1. How many tiles in term 4?
In y = ax + b, what does the number a represent?
flashcards.back: The rate of change: how much y grows for each unit of x, like rupees per GB.

flashcards.front: Telecom bill: 10 GB cost Rs 350, 20 GB cost Rs 550. Find a and b.
Gym: 10 court-hours cost Rs 800, 15 hours cost Rs 1100, bill y = ax + b. Find a.
flashcards.back: a = 60, since 1100 - 800 = 300 over 5 extra hours gives Rs 60 per hour.

flashcards.front: What is the fewest number of points needed to plot a straight line?
flashcards.back: Two. Find any two points, plot them, join with a ruler and extend both ways.

flashcards.front: For y = 2x + 1, which point comes from x = 0?
flashcards.back: The point A (0, 1): when x = 0, y = 2 × 0 + 1 = 1.

flashcards.front: How do you verify that (7, 15) lies on the line y = 2x + 1?
flashcards.back: Substitute x = 7 and y = 15 into the equation: 2 × 7 + 1 = 15, so the point satisfies it.

flashcards.front: The points (1, 3), (3, 9), (4, 12) lie on one line. What is its equation?
flashcards.back: y = 3x, because each y-coordinate is three times the x-coordinate.

flashcards.front: Points (-3, 6), (0, 0), (3, -6) lie on y = -2x. What does negative a do to the graph?
flashcards.back: It makes the line slope downward as x increases, the picture of linear decay.

examples.title: Two Numbers That Sum to 64
examples.problem: The sum of two numbers is 64. One of the numbers is 10 more than the other. Find the two numbers. (Example 6 in the book.)
steps: Let the smaller number be x. Then the larger number is x + 10.
Their sum is 64, so x + (x + 10) = 64, which simplifies to the linear equation 2x + 10 = 64.
Move the constant across: 2x = 64 - 10 = 54.
Divide by 2: x = 27, so the larger number is x + 10 = 37.
Check: 27 + 37 = 64 and 37 - 27 = 10, exactly as the problem says.

examples.title: Cracking the Telecom Bill
examples.problem: A telecom company charges a fixed monthly fee plus a cost per GB of data. A student observes that using 10 GB costs Rs 350 and using 20 GB costs Rs 550. If the bill is y = ax + b, find a and b. (Example 11 in the book.)
steps: Substitute the two observations into y = ax + b to get 350 = 10a + b and 550 = 20a + b.
From the first equation, write b = 350 - 10a.
Substitute into the second equation: 550 = 20a + (350 - 10a).
Simplify: 550 = 10a + 350, so 10a = 200 and a = 20.
The 20 is the cost per GB of data and the 150 is the fixed monthly fee.
examples.answer: a = 20 and b = 150, so the monthly bill is y = 20x + 150 rupees.

examples.title: Journey Cost Questions
examples.problem: The cost of a journey is C(d) = 100 + 60d rupees, where d is the distance travelled in km. Find the cost of travelling 15 km, and find the distance for which the cost is Rs 700. (Think and Reflect questions of Example 9.)
steps: For 15 km, substitute d = 15 into C(d) = 100 + 60d.
Compute 60 × 15 = 900, so C = 100 + 900 = 1000 rupees.
For the second part, start from the linear equation 100 + 60d = 700.
Subtract 100 from both sides: 60d = 600.
Divide by 60: d = 10 km.
examples.answer: Travelling 15 km costs Rs 1000, and a journey costing Rs 700 covers 10 km.

examples.title: From Plotted Points to Equation
examples.problem: The points (-1, -3), (0, 0), (1, 3), (3, 9) and (4, 12) are plotted and joined with a ruler, and all five lie on one straight line. Find the equation of the line and verify a point on it. (Example 12 in the book.)
steps: Compare y with x at each point: -3 = 3 × (-1), 0 = 3 × 0, 3 = 3 × 1, 9 = 3 × 3, 12 = 3 × 4.
In every case the y-coordinate is three times the x-coordinate.
So the rule connecting the coordinates is y = 3x.
Verify by substitution, the same method used for (7, 15) on y = 2x + 1: for the point (3, 9), check 3 × 3 = 9, which is true.
examples.answer: The line is y = 3x, and every point on it satisfies this equation.

steps.label: Meet expressions
steps.detail: Raju's boxes and the garden fence turn stories into terms.

steps.label: Name the parts
steps.detail: Spot terms, variables, coefficients and constants.

steps.label: Notice the pattern
steps.detail: Successive values differ by a constant: a linear pattern.

steps.label: Classify the change
steps.detail: Constant increase is growth, constant decrease is decay.

steps.label: Form the equation
steps.detail: Equate the polynomial to a constant, or set y = ax + b.

steps.label: Solve for unknowns
steps.detail: Find x, or use two observations to find a and b.

steps.label: Draw the line
steps.detail: Plot two points, join them, extend both ways.
